JAPAN UNFOLDED
Fuji Manga Places Meet Yuji
Summer after dark · Northern Japan

When paper, light and a love story take over two cities.

Aomori’s Nebuta and Sendai’s Tanabata are often grouped as famous Tohoku festivals. Stand inside them and they feel like entirely different universes.

Summer in northern Japan does not arrive quietly. In Aomori, enormous illuminated figures advance through the street. In Sendai, shopping arcades disappear beneath forests of streamers. Both are called matsuri. That is where the similarity ends.

Nebuta: drawings that learned to move

Aomori Nebuta’s giant lantern floats turn warriors, myths and dramatic expressions into luminous sculpture. The scale is the first shock. The second is movement: light shifts across folded surfaces while music and dancers pull the crowd into the procession. The main festival is traditionally held August 2–7; always confirm current official dates and viewing rules.

Each float begins long before the parade. Nebuta artists plan the design, form three-dimensional structures and stretch paper across complex frames before colour and internal light bring the figure forward. The result looks solid from a distance and impossibly delicate up close: a huge warrior, dragon or wave built from materials that still reveal the craft of the hand.

The sound prevents the spectacle from becoming a silent exhibition. Drums, flutes and calls create a rhythm that reaches you before the float does. Haneto dancers add another layer of movement. The street becomes a collaboration between makers, musicians, dancers, pullers and spectators rather than a row of illuminated objects.

Tanabata: a sky story brought down to eye level

Tanabata grows from the legend of star-crossed Orihime and Hikoboshi. In Sendai, elaborate bamboo decorations and long streamers transform familiar streets. Instead of one object moving past you, the city becomes something you move through.

The decorations are not random colour. Traditional forms carry wishes—for study, skill, health, prosperity and protection. Shops and communities compete through craftsmanship, but the effect at walking speed is surprisingly intimate. Paper brushes your field of vision. The ceiling of an ordinary arcade drops into a floating forest.

One festival sends a story toward you. The other makes you push gently through the story.

The useful surprise: don’t ask which festival is “better.” Choose your verb. At Nebuta, you watch the story charge toward you. At Sendai Tanabata, you walk inside it.

Why Tohoku summer feels so intense

Part of the emotional force comes from compression. These nights are prepared across months and experienced across a small number of summer days. Visitors see the finished spectacle; local participants also see meetings, rehearsals, repairs, neighbourhood pride and the knowledge that everything will soon come down.

That temporary quality is not a weakness. It is the pulse of matsuri culture. You cannot store the whole event in a photograph because sound, crowd movement, humidity and anticipation are part of the work.

Travel with respect

These are living community events, not theme-park sets. Follow barriers and staff instructions, ask before taking close portraits, and leave room for local participants. A camera can capture light; attention captures what the light means.

Dates and access change. Check official festival and local tourism sites before booking.
